reference.source: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID) / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthesis caused by PTS mutations; it is the most common cause of BH4-deficient hyperphenylalaninaemia

It presents as hyperphenylalaninaemia detected on newborn screening but, unlike classic phenylketonuria, dietary phenylalanine restriction alone does not prevent neurological deterioration because central monoamine synthesis is also impaired
BH4 is the cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase as well as tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylases, so deficiency causes both elevated phenylalanine and reduced dopamine and serotonin
Untreated infants develop progressive encephalopathy with dystonia, hypotonia or hypertonia, oculogyric crises, seizures, and developmental delay despite phenylalanine control
Management combines BH4 (cofactor) supplementation to lower phenylalanine with levodopa and a serotonin precursor to replace the deficient neurotransmitters, sometimes with folinic acid

Every infant with hyperphenylalaninaemia should be evaluated for a BH4 defect (pterin profile and dihydropteridine reductase activity) so that treatable cofactor and neurotransmitter deficiencies are not missed
reference.pathophysiology: 6-pyruvoyl-tetrahydropterin synthase catalyses the second step of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) biosynthesis. Biallelic PTS mutations reduce BH4, the obligatory cofactor for phenylalanine hydroxylase, tyrosine hydroxylase, and tryptophan hydroxylase. Consequently phenylalanine accumulates (hyperphenylalaninaemia) while central synthesis of dopamine and serotonin falls. The dual insult explains why treating the amino-acid abnormality alone is insufficient: the neurotransmitter deficiency drives a progressive movement disorder and encephalopathy. The pterin profile shows raised neopterin with low biopterin, reflecting the enzymatic block, and this pattern helps distinguish it from other BH4 defects.
additionalDifferentials: Other neurotransmitter disorders causing infantile dystonia and encephalopathy
additionalInvestigations: Urine and blood pterin profile showing raised neopterin with low biopterin
Dihydropteridine reductase activity assay (normal, to exclude the recycling defect)
Blood phenylalanine and a BH4 loading test demonstrating phenylalanine lowering
PTS gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis
Cerebrospinal fluid neurotransmitter metabolites (low homovanillic and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid)
Developmental and neurological assessment with EEG if seizures occur
redFlags: Neurological deterioration despite adequate phenylalanine control, indicating an untreated cofactor/neurotransmitter defect
Progressive dystonia, oculogyric crises, or seizures in an infant with hyperphenylalaninaemia
Failure to screen a hyperphenylalaninaemic newborn for a BH4 disorder
Feeding and swallowing difficulty from evolving encephalopathy
reference.prognosis: With early and combined treatment (cofactor supplementation plus neurotransmitter precursors) neurological outcome can be good, but delayed or incomplete therapy leads to persistent movement disorder, cognitive impairment, and disability. Lifelong specialist metabolic follow-up is required.
pitfalls: Treating a raised phenylalanine as classic phenylketonuria without excluding a BH4 defect
Relying on phenylalanine restriction alone and neglecting the neurotransmitter deficiency
Not measuring pterins and dihydropteridine reductase activity to subtype the disorder
Under-dosing or delaying neurotransmitter-precursor therapy while focusing on amino-acid control
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID)
management: Tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor supplementation with sapropterin as the mainstay to correct the hyperphenylalaninaemia, since dietary phenylalanine restriction alone does not prevent neurological deterioration.
Central neurotransmitter replacement with levodopa combined with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor and a serotonin precursor to restore dopamine and serotonin.
Folinic acid supplementation as an adjunct to support central folate metabolism.
Symptomatic management of the movement disorder, dystonia and any seizures.
Monitoring of blood phenylalanine, cerebrospinal fluid neurotransmitter metabolites and developmental and neurological progress.
Lifelong specialist metabolic and neurology follow-up as part of multidisciplinary care.
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder, with confirmatory PTS testing and family screening.
